skills.title: Measuring Length
skills.summary: Length is measured in units such as millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers. Each metric unit is ten or more times larger than the one before, so you convert by multiplying or dividing by powers of ten. Choose a unit that fits the size of the object.
objectives: Choose a suitable metric unit for a length.
Convert between metric length units.
Compare two lengths.

skills.title: Measuring Mass
skills.summary: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in units such as milligrams, grams, and kilograms. As with length, metric mass units are related by powers of ten: 1000 mg make a gram and 1000 g make a kilogram.
objectives: Choose a suitable metric unit for a mass.
Convert between metric mass units.
Compare two masses.

skills.title: Measuring Time
skills.summary: Time is measured in units such as seconds, minutes, and hours. Unlike length and mass, time is not based on tens: 60 seconds make a minute and 60 minutes make an hour. Converting uses these factors of 60.
objectives: Convert between seconds, minutes, and hours.
Choose a suitable unit for a duration.
Find an elapsed time.

skills.title: Measuring Temperature
skills.summary: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is, often in degrees Celsius. Water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. Temperatures below freezing are negative, so working with temperature change uses integer addition and subtraction.
objectives: Read and compare temperatures, including negatives.
Find a temperature change.
Relate freezing and boiling points of water.

skills.title: Area
skills.summary: Area is the amount of flat surface a shape covers, measured in square units. The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, and the area of a square is a side times itself. Area is always given in square units, like square centimeters.
objectives: Compute the area of a rectangle.
Compute the area of a square.
State that area uses square units.

skills.title: Volume
skills.summary: Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. The volume of a box (rectangular prism) is length times width times height, and the volume of a cube is a side multiplied by itself three times.
objectives: Compute the volume of a box.
Compute the volume of a cube.
State that volume uses cubic units.

skills.title: Unit Conversion
skills.summary: Converting between metric units means multiplying or dividing by a power of ten (for length and mass) or by 60 (for time). Going to a smaller unit multiplies, and going to a larger unit divides.
objectives: Convert length and mass across metric units.
Convert time units.
Decide whether to multiply or divide when converting.

skills.title: Estimation and Reasonableness
skills.summary: Estimation gives a quick, approximate answer by rounding numbers or using benchmarks, and it helps you judge whether a result or a measurement is reasonable. A door about 2 meters tall is reasonable; 2 kilometers is not.
objectives: Estimate a calculation by rounding.
Judge whether a measurement is reasonable.
Choose a sensible benchmark for a size.

components.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to choose length units, convert between them, and compare lengths.
Recall place value and multiplying or dividing by 10 and 100. Metric conversions use these directly.

You measure a pencil in centimeters, a room in meters, and a journey in kilometers, choosing a unit that gives a convenient number. The metric system is built on tens: 10 mm make a centimeter, 100 cm make a meter, 1000 m make a kilometer.

Common metric length units are the millimeter (mm), centimeter (cm), meter (m), and kilometer (km). Conversions: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m. Multiply to go to smaller units, divide to go to larger units.
Convert 2 meters to centimeters. Since 1 m = 100 cm, multiply: 2 times 100 = 200 cm.
Convert 500 cm to meters. Since 100 cm = 1 m, divide: 500 divided by 100 = 5 m.
A common mistake is multiplying when you should divide. Going to a smaller unit multiplies (more of them fit); going to a larger unit divides.
Length uses mm, cm, m, and km, related by powers of ten. Multiply to convert to smaller units and divide to convert to larger ones; pick a unit that suits the object.
How many centimeters are in 3 meters, and how did you convert?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to choose mass units, convert between them, and compare masses.
Recall multiplying and dividing by 1000, and how metric length units scaled by powers of ten. Mass works the same way.
You weigh a feather in grams, a person in kilograms, and a grain of medicine in milligrams. The metric system links them by thousands: 1000 mg make a gram, and 1000 g make a kilogram.
Common metric mass units are the milligram (mg), gram (g), and kilogram (kg). Conversions: 1 g = 1000 mg and 1 kg = 1000 g. Multiply to convert to smaller units and divide to convert to larger units.
Convert 2 kilograms to grams. Since 1 kg = 1000 g, multiply: 2 times 1000 = 2000 g.
Convert 500 grams to kilograms. Since 1000 g = 1 kg, divide: 500 divided by 1000 = 0.5 kg.
A common mistake is confusing grams and kilograms, which differ by a factor of 1000. Always check which unit is larger before converting.
Mass uses mg, g, and kg, related by thousands. Multiply to convert to smaller units and divide to convert to larger ones.
How many grams are in 3 kilograms, and how did you convert?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to convert between seconds, minutes, and hours and find elapsed times.
Recall your multiplication and division facts. Time conversions use 60, not powers of ten.
A clock reminds us that time units are grouped by 60: sixty seconds fill a minute, and sixty minutes fill an hour. So 2 minutes is 2 groups of 60 seconds, which is 120 seconds.
Common time units are the second (s), minute (min), and hour (h). Conversions: 1 min = 60 s and 1 h = 60 min. Multiply to convert to smaller units and divide to convert to larger units.
Convert 2 minutes to seconds. Since 1 min = 60 s, multiply: 2 times 60 = 120 s.
Convert 2 hours to minutes. Since 1 h = 60 min, multiply: 2 times 60 = 120 min.
A common mistake is converting time as if it used 100 instead of 60. Remember that an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
Time uses seconds, minutes, and hours, related by 60. Multiply to convert to smaller units and divide to convert to larger ones.
How many seconds are in 3 minutes, and what factor did you use?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to compare temperatures and calculate temperature changes, including below zero.
Recall adding and subtracting integers. A temperature below zero is a negative number, and a change is a difference.
A thermometer is a vertical number line. On the Celsius scale, water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. A cold winter day might be -5 degrees, five below freezing.

Temperature in degrees Celsius uses 0 for the freezing point of water and 100 for the boiling point. A rise is a positive change and a drop is a negative change; the amount of change is found by subtracting the two temperatures.
The temperature is 5 degrees and drops 8 degrees. The new temperature is 5 - 8 = -3 degrees, three below freezing.
The temperature rises from -5 degrees to 3 degrees. The change is 3 - (-5) = 3 + 5 = 8 degrees warmer.
A common mistake is ignoring the sign when crossing zero. Use integer rules: dropping below zero gives a negative temperature, and a rise from a negative adds.
Temperature is measured in degrees, with water freezing at 0 and boiling at 100. Negative temperatures are below freezing, and changes are found by subtracting, using integer rules.
If it is 2 degrees and the temperature falls 6 degrees, what is the new temperature?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to find the area of rectangles and squares and label it in square units.
Recall multiplication and that a rectangle can be seen as rows and columns of unit squares.

Cover a rectangle with unit squares. A rectangle 3 cm by 4 cm holds 3 rows of 4 squares, which is 12 squares, so its area is 12 square centimeters. Multiplying length by width counts these squares quickly.

Area is the amount of surface a flat shape covers, measured in square units. For a rectangle, area = length times width. For a square, area = side times side. Units are squared, such as square centimeters.
A rectangle is 3 cm by 4 cm. Its area is 3 times 4 = 12 square centimeters.
A square has a side of 5 cm. Its area is 5 times 5 = 25 square centimeters.
A common mistake is adding the sides instead of multiplying (that gives perimeter, not area), or forgetting to use square units.
Area measures surface in square units. Rectangle area is length times width; square area is side times side.
What is the area of a rectangle 6 m by 2 m, and why is it in square meters?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to find the volume of boxes and cubes and label it in cubic units.
Recall area as length times width. Volume extends this by one more dimension, height.
Fill a box with unit cubes. A box 2 by 3 by 4 holds a bottom layer of 2 times 3 = 6 cubes, and there are 4 such layers, giving 24 cubes. So its volume is 24 cubic units.

Volume is the space a solid occupies, measured in cubic units. For a box (rectangular prism), volume = length times width times height. For a cube, volume = side times side times side. Units are cubed, such as cubic centimeters.
A box is 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm. Its volume is 2 times 3 times 4 = 24 cubic centimeters.
A cube has a side of 3 cm. Its volume is 3 times 3 times 3 = 27 cubic centimeters.
A common mistake is using square units for volume or multiplying only two dimensions. Volume needs all three dimensions and cubic units.
Volume measures space in cubic units. Box volume is length times width times height; cube volume is side times side times side.
What is the volume of a box 5 by 2 by 2 cm, and why is it in cubic centimeters?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to convert measurements between units and decide whether to multiply or divide.
Recall the metric relationships: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 kg = 1000 g, and 1 min = 60 s, 1 h = 60 min.

A smaller unit needs more of them to make the same amount, so converting to a smaller unit multiplies. A larger unit needs fewer, so converting to a larger unit divides. 4 km is many meters (4000), but 2500 mg is only a few grams (2.5).

To convert to a smaller unit, multiply by the conversion factor; to convert to a larger unit, divide by it. The factor is a power of ten for metric length and mass, and 60 for the second-minute-hour steps of time.
Convert 4 kilometers to meters. Meters are smaller, so multiply by 1000: 4 times 1000 = 4000 m.
Convert 250 centimeters to meters. Meters are larger, so divide by 100: 250 divided by 100 = 2.5 m.
A common mistake is multiplying when you should divide. Ask whether the new unit is smaller (multiply) or larger (divide) than the old one.
Convert to a smaller unit by multiplying and to a larger unit by dividing, using the correct factor (a power of ten for length and mass, 60 for time).
To convert meters to centimeters, do you multiply or divide, and by what?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to estimate calculations and judge whether measurements are reasonable.
Recall rounding to the nearest ten or hundred, which makes numbers easier to work with in your head.

Before trusting an answer, a quick estimate acts as a sanity check. To estimate 48 times 2, round 48 to 50 and get about 100. And common sense says a door is about 2 meters tall, not 2 centimeters or 2 kilometers.

Estimation replaces numbers with nearby round numbers, or uses known benchmarks, to get an approximate result quickly. A measurement is reasonable when its size matches a sensible benchmark for the object.
Estimate 19 + 22. Round 19 to 20 and 22 to 20; the estimate is 20 + 20 = 40. The exact answer, 41, is close, so 40 is a good estimate.
Estimate 302 - 99 by rounding to 300 - 100. The estimate is 200, close to the exact 203.
A common mistake is choosing an unreasonable unit or benchmark, like saying an apple has a mass of 150 kilograms. Compare with a familiar object to check reasonableness.
Estimation uses rounding or benchmarks for a quick approximate answer and a reasonableness check. A good estimate is close to the exact value and matches sensible benchmarks.
About how tall is a typical door, and how would you estimate 48 times 2?
